variants: HID-emulating (BadUSB-style) variant where the device presents as a keyboard and types a benign, logged command rather than relying on autorun of stored files.
Branded/context-specific variant using packaging consistent with a plausible source (a conference giveaway, a courier envelope) rather than a plain unlabeled drive.
Charging-cable variant (a modified cable rather than a drive) testing the same curiosity-driven behavior via a different physical form factor.
Mail-delivered variant testing whether a USB drive arriving by internal mail with a plausible cover letter is treated differently from one found in a parking lot.
mitigation: Disable autorun/autoplay for removable media at the endpoint policy level across the fleet.
Deploy USB device control (allow-listing known, organization-issued media; blocking or alerting on unknown mass-storage and HID devices) via endpoint protection or a dedicated DLP agent.
Train staff explicitly on found-media handling: hand it to security/IT rather than plugging it into any work (or personal) device.
Provide a simple, low-friction reporting path for found media, mirroring the phishing-report button's ease of use.
Ensure security operations has alerting for unexpected new removable-storage or HID-device events on managed endpoints, independent of this specific test.
Periodically repeat this assessment, since susceptibility often changes meaningfully after the first awareness campaign addressing it specifically.

Extend the same media-control policy to any air-gapped or industrial-control environments in scope, where removable media is often a primary infection vector precisely because network-based defenses don't apply.
SOCIAL-012.mitigationClientFacing: USB devices left in your car park and common areas were picked up and connected to company computers. Curiosity is the mechanism, and a device labelled with something that looks internal is more likely to be plugged in than one that is not. A device like this can act as a keyboard and type commands at machine speed the moment it is connected, so the user does not need to open a file for it to work. The most effective control is technical rather than behavioural: restrict which USB device types are permitted through your endpoint management, which stops the attack regardless of who picks the device up. Pair it with clear guidance that unknown devices go to IT, not into a machine.

SOCIAL-013.prerequisites: Written authorization to observe unattended workstations in open areas and, where explicitly permitted, to briefly approach an unlocked, unattended machine to confirm the session is genuinely active (without entering credentials, opening files, or taking any action beyond confirming the lock state). No special tooling required beyond observation and timing.
SOCIAL-013.whatItIs: This checks whether the company's screen-lock timeout is actually enforced by policy — and, just as importantly, whether people actually respect it. If an employee steps away from their desk, does the machine sit unlocked and exposed to anyone walking by until the timeout kicks in? Or does it never lock at all because someone's turned that setting off?
SOCIAL-013.rootCause: An already-unlocked session has no further login check standing between a random passerby and everything on that screen. If the timeout is set too long, applied inconsistently across different device types, or routinely disabled by employees for convenience, the control looks fine on paper but doesn't actually protect anything in practice.
SOCIAL-013.impact: A walk-up attacker inherits the full access of the logged-in user instantly: email, file shares, internal systems. No exploitation effort is needed at all. And because no credential was used, monitoring tuned to watch for unusual authentication events has nothing to alert on.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the organization's configured group policy or MDM setting for screen-lock inactivity timeout, and compare it against the value actually observed on a sample of real workstations.
Observe open work areas during natural break periods (lunch, coffee runs, meetings) for unattended, unlocked screens rather than relying on policy documentation alone.
Check whether the timeout is applied consistently across device types (desktop, laptop, kiosk/shared terminal) or whether some categories are exempted or misconfigured.
Assess whether employees have a habit of manually locking (Windows+L / Control+Command+Q) when stepping away briefly, independent of the automatic timeout.
Review whether shared or kiosk-style terminals (reception desks, shared lab machines) have an appropriately shorter timeout given their higher walk-up exposure.

Identify any process or technical exception (a long-running batch job, a presentation display) that legitimately requires a longer timeout, so the finding can distinguish a genuine business exception from an unmanaged gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW's authorization to observe and, if permitted, briefly approach an unattended unlocked workstation solely to confirm and time the lock state — not to interact with any application or data.
During normal business activity, observe unattended workstations and record the elapsed time from the employee stepping away to either a manual lock, an automatic lock, or continued exposure.

Where approach is authorized, confirm the session is genuinely active (rather than already locked and merely appearing active from a distance) without touching the keyboard/mouse beyond what's needed to observe the lock indicator.
Do not open any application, file, or browser tab, and do not move the mouse in a way that could be mistaken for actual use of the session.
If the employee returns during observation, disengage naturally without drawing attention, consistent with a passive-observation methodology.

Record the specific device/location pattern (desk type, department, device category) rather than only an aggregate exposure count, since remediation is often device-type-specific (e.g. kiosk terminals need a shorter timeout than the general fleet).

variants: Shared/kiosk-terminal variant specifically targeting reception desks, lab machines, or conference-room displays that are more frequently walked away from by multiple different users.
Remote-work variant assessing whether a home-office setup has any equivalent physical-presence exposure (e.g. a shared household space) distinct from the office environment.
Privileged-user variant specifically observing IT/administrative staff workstations, where an exposed session carries materially higher impact than a standard user's.
Meeting-room variant assessing whether a workstation or display left connected and unlocked after a meeting exposes the previous presenter's session to the next group entering the room.
mitigation: Set and enforce a screen-lock inactivity timeout appropriate to risk level via centralized policy (group policy/MDM) rather than relying on device-local settings employees can change.
Apply a materially shorter timeout to shared/kiosk terminals and privileged-user workstations than the general employee fleet.
Train and normalize a manual-lock habit (a simple keyboard shortcut) as the primary control, treating the automatic timeout as a backstop rather than the sole mechanism.
Audit configured timeout values periodically across device types and correct drift or undocumented exceptions.
Consider proximity-based automatic locking (Bluetooth-paired-device or badge-based) for high-risk workstations, which locks the instant the employee steps away rather than after a fixed delay.
Include this specific behavior in security-awareness training with a concrete, memorable framing (what a walk-up attacker gains in the exposure window) rather than an abstract policy reminder.
Ensure any documented business exception to the standard timeout (a long-running process, a presentation display) has a compensating control rather than simply being exempted from the policy.
SOCIAL-013.mitigationClientFacing: Unattended computers were found unlocked and logged in, in areas where a visitor could reach them. Anyone sitting down at one has the full access of that employee, with everything they do recorded under that person's name — which makes an incident both easy to carry out and hard to attribute afterwards. Shorten the automatic lock timeout through central policy so it does not depend on people remembering, and make locking the screen a visible norm that managers model themselves. Where staff complain the timeout interrupts their work, that is worth listening to: a timeout set so short that people work around it is less effective than a slightly longer one that they accept.

SOCIAL-014.prerequisites: Written authorization defining the target population, approved pretext theme(s), and what constitutes success (information disclosed vs. action taken), plus a pre-agreed disclosure/safe-word procedure. A phone/VoIP line, and ideally an OSINT dossier from a prior phase to make the pretext realistic; note that call-ID spoofing carries jurisdiction-specific legal restrictions and requires its own explicit authorization if used at all.
SOCIAL-014.whatItIs: Vishing tests whether employees give up sensitive information, or take an action they're asked to, during a live phone call from someone pretending to be a trusted person — internal IT, a vendor, an executive's assistant. Unlike the help-desk pretext (SOCIAL-002) or the IT remote-access pretext (SOCIAL-007), this covers a broader range of asks: org details, someone's schedule, a minor policy exception — not one specific goal like a password reset.
SOCIAL-014.rootCause: A phone call carries a lot of unearned trust — a confident tone, the right jargon, a bit of urgency — and there's essentially no equivalent to email's sender-verification systems for voice calls. Most security-awareness training has spent years focused on email, so employees rarely apply the same level of caution to a phone call.
SOCIAL-014.impact: A successful call extracts organisational detail that feeds a later, more damaging attack — a name to drop in the next pretext, a confirmed absence to exploit in a payment fraud attempt. It can also secure a small but real policy exception outright. It is harder to investigate than phishing too, since it leaves no artefact for the security team to examine afterwards.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the specific information-disclosure or action goals in scope for this test, distinguishing it clearly from the help-desk-reset and IT-remote-access pretexts covered elsewhere.
Review whether the organization has any documented process for verifying an unfamiliar caller's identity before disclosing internal information.
Assess whether call-recording or call-logging exists for the target department, which would help characterize baseline vishing exposure even outside this specific test.
Identify a representative population across departments (reception, HR, finance, IT) rather than testing a single team, since susceptibility and information-disclosure risk vary meaningfully by role.
Check whether employees are trained to distinguish reasonable external inquiries (a real vendor callback) from social-engineering pretexts using the same channel.
Establish clear success/failure criteria (information disclosed, action taken, or call correctly declined/escalated) before testing begins.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the SOW's authorized target population, pretext theme, and information/action goal, along with the disclosure procedure to use once a call demonstrates the finding.
Build the pretext from previously-authorized OSINT, avoiding any pretext that would require impersonating a real, named external individual without separate specific authorization to do so.
Place the call with a plausible, moderately confident persona and record whether the employee verifies the caller's identity before disclosing information or taking the requested action.
Stop at the point the goal is demonstrated (information was disclosed, or the employee agreed to the requested minor action) rather than pushing further than needed to establish the finding.
Disclose the test to the employee promptly and supportively once the call concludes or once the finding is established, whichever is appropriate to the specific scenario.
Repeat across the representative population sample identified during discovery, varying department and pretext urgency, to characterize the finding as a pattern rather than an individual result.
Where call recording is in scope and legally permitted in the relevant jurisdiction, retain only what's needed to substantiate specific findings in the report.

variants: Executive-assistant targeting variant seeking schedule/travel information to support a later business-email-compromise attempt.
Vendor-impersonation variant requesting a minor process exception (an early invoice payment confirmation, a shipping address change) rather than pure information disclosure.
Multi-call chained variant where an initial low-sensitivity call (confirming a name or department) is used to add credibility to a follow-up call to a different employee.

Voice-cloning-adjacent awareness variant, discussing (without necessarily deploying) how synthetic-voice tools could impersonate a specific known executive's voice in a future engagement phase, to inform the client's risk register even where this specific test doesn't use one.
mitigation: Establish a documented, trained caller-verification process for any request involving internal information or a process exception, independent of how confident or familiar the caller sounds.
Provide employees a simple, non-confrontational way to defer a request to a verifiable channel (a ticket, a callback to a known number) without feeling they've been unhelpful.
Train staff specifically on vishing patterns distinct from email-phishing training, since the trust cues and available verification signals differ meaningfully between the two channels.
Extend the organization's phishing-simulation program to include a recurring vishing component, rather than treating voice as an untested channel.
Log and review call patterns for departments handling sensitive information (finance, HR, IT) to establish a baseline that could surface real vishing attempts.
Recognize and positively reinforce employees who correctly verify or decline a suspicious call, consistent with the same principle applied to email and help-desk pretexting.
As synthetic-voice technology matures, begin evaluating voice-cloning-resistant verification steps (a shared, rotating verbal passphrase for high-sensitivity requests) for the highest-risk roles.
SOCIAL-014.mitigationClientFacing: A phone call is persuasive in a way an email is not. There is a live person, a reason to answer now, and no opportunity to re-read the request or ask a colleague. Our calls tested whether staff would disclose information or take an action on the strength of a plausible caller. The control that works is a pause rather than a rule about what to say: any request involving credentials, access changes or payments is confirmed by calling back on a number from your own directory. Make it explicitly acceptable to end a call and check, including with someone senior. Attackers rely on the reluctance to be seen doubting an executive, so leadership publicly endorsing the callback rule is a genuine control.

SOCIAL-015.prerequisites: Written authorization explicitly naming BEC/financial-fraud pretext testing as in scope, including which finance/AP staff may be targeted and a hard cap on any simulated transaction amount. Sign-off from finance leadership on the exact wording of the simulated request and confirmation that no real funds will move even if the target complies. A spoofable or look-alike sender identity (with client IT's cooperation — e.g., a cousin domain or a From-header spoof test account) and knowledge of the organization's actual approval chain for wire transfers, gathered from the scoping call or public sources (OSINT-style, overlapping with SOCIAL-001).
SOCIAL-015.whatItIs: Business Email Compromise is a targeted attack where the tester poses as a senior executive, or a trusted outsider such as a lawyer or auditor, over email. They instruct someone in Accounts Payable to make an urgent, confidential wire transfer or to change a vendor's banking details. The framing does the work: urgency, authority, and 'keep this quiet' together push the target past the normal approval steps.
SOCIAL-015.rootCause: The company's process for approving wire transfers or vendor banking changes relies on whether the email 'looks right' to the person reading it, instead of requiring an independent, out-of-band confirmation — like calling a phone number that was already on file, not one provided in the email — before any money moves.
SOCIAL-015.impact: A successful attack of this kind moves money out of the organisation directly, and the FBI's IC3 consistently ranks it among the highest-dollar-loss cybercrime categories. Unlike most social engineering findings, the impact is immediate, quantifiable and visible at board level rather than a downstream security consequence. It is also frequently the final objective of a broader campaign rather than a step toward something else.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm with the client exactly which finance/AP staff and which type of request (wire transfer vs. vendor banking-detail change) are in scope, and agree a hard-cap simulated amount and a same-day debrief commitment regardless of outcome.
Identify a plausible executive to impersonate (CFO, CEO, or a known outside counsel/vendor contact) using OSINT (org chart, LinkedIn, press releases) to make the pretext specific and credible.

Determine the organization's stated approval/verification process for wire transfers (from policy documents provided in scoping, or by asking finance directly as part of a legitimate process review) so the test can specifically probe whether that process is actually followed under pressure.

Check whether email authentication controls (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) would flag a spoofed or look-alike sender domain, since this affects whether the pretext needs a genuine spoof or can rely on a display-name trick alone.

Confirm whether the target's mail client visibly displays the full sender address or only a display name by default, since display-name-only rendering significantly raises susceptibility to a look-alike domain.
Establish the out-of-band verification channel (phone number) that SHOULD be used to confirm such a request, so the test can specifically check whether the target attempts it before acting.
exploitationSteps: Confirm final wording and target(s) with the client sign-off obtained during scoping, and never exceed the agreed simulated transaction cap under any circumstance.

Send a pretext email impersonating the chosen executive or trusted third party, using urgency and confidentiality framing consistent with real BEC campaigns (e.g., 'time-sensitive, don't discuss with the team yet').
Request either a wire transfer to a test account explicitly provided by the client for this purpose, or a vendor banking-detail change to a test record, never a real destination.

If the target requests verification, observe whether they attempt the correct out-of-band channel (calling a known-good number) versus replying to the same email thread or calling a number provided within the pretext email itself (the latter is a fail — the attacker-controlled channel would just confirm the fraud).

If the target proceeds without any verification, stop immediately once compliance is confirmed (e.g., they reply 'processing now') — do not need to see an actual transaction execute, and immediately disclose the test to the target's manager per the engagement's real-time-fail protocol.

Document the full timeline: time to open, time to reply/act, whether verification was attempted and through which channel, and whether the request matched a known amount/wording pattern that should have raised suspicion.

examplePayloads.label: Urgent CEO wire-request pretext (opening line)
examplePayloads.command: Hi [Name], I'm in back-to-back meetings and need you to process a time-sensitive wire today — please keep this confidential until I brief the team. Can you confirm you're able to action this in the next hour?

examplePayloads.label: Confidentiality/urgency framing follow-up
examplePayloads.command: This relates to a pending acquisition, so please don't loop in anyone else yet — I'll explain fully once we're through this. Let me know once it's sent.

examplePayloads.label: Vendor banking-detail change pretext (as 'accounts payable' contact)
examplePayloads.command: Please note our banking details have changed as of this week due to a transition in our finance provider — attached is the updated remittance form for future payments.

examplePayloads.label: Attacker-controlled 'verification' number embedded in pretext (fail condition if used)
examplePayloads.command: If you need to confirm, you can reach me directly on my direct line: [test-controlled number] — easier than email right now.

examplePayloads.label: Reply-thread pressure escalation (if initial request stalls)
examplePayloads.command: Just checking in — this needs to go out before end of day, can you prioritize it? Happy to jump on a quick call if that's faster.

examplePayloads.label: Look-alike domain construction (for authorized spoof testing only)
examplePayloads.command: ceo@corp-finance-group.com  (cousin domain of the real corp-financegroup.com, differing by a hyphen)

variants: Vendor Email Compromise, where the pretext impersonates a genuine existing supplier rather than an internal executive, requesting a banking-detail update for an upcoming legitimate invoice.
Legal/M&A-pretext BEC, leaning on a plausible pending-acquisition or litigation cover story to justify unusual secrecy and urgency.
Payroll-diversion BEC, targeting HR/payroll staff to redirect an employee's direct-deposit details rather than a vendor payment.
Gift-card BEC, a lower-dollar but very common variant asking an employee to urgently purchase gift cards 'for a client' and send the codes.
mitigation: Require mandatory out-of-band verification (a callback to a previously-known, independently-sourced phone number — never one provided in the request itself) for any wire transfer or vendor banking-detail change, with no exceptions regardless of seniority or urgency framing.

Implement DMARC enforcement (p=reject or at minimum p=quarantine) alongside SPF and DKIM to block exact-domain spoofing, and deploy look-alike-domain monitoring to catch cousin-domain registrations targeting the organization.
Configure email clients to always display the full sender address, not just the display name, and apply an external-sender banner so a spoofed 'internal-looking' email is visibly flagged.
Set a hard secondary-approval threshold (dual authorization) for wire transfers and banking-detail changes above a defined dollar amount, independent of any single approver's judgment.

Run recurring BEC-specific awareness training for finance/AP staff specifically, distinct from general phishing training, since BEC pretexts exploit authority and urgency rather than malicious links or attachments.

Establish a clear, no-blame reporting culture so an employee who suspects a BEC attempt (even after acting on it) reports immediately rather than staying silent out of embarrassment — time-to-detection is the main lever for fund recovery.
SOCIAL-015.mitigationClientFacing: This tests whether a payment request that appears to come from a senior executive would actually be paid. These attacks do not involve malware and there is nothing for your email filtering to catch — the message is just text, usually urgent, usually confidential, usually timed for when the named executive is known to be travelling. Losses are frequently large and recovery is rare once funds have moved internationally. The control is a payment process that does not depend on anyone's judgement about whether an email is genuine: out-of-band verbal confirmation for any new payee or changed bank details, a second approver above a threshold, and an explicit rule that urgency and confidentiality never justify skipping either. Make it clear that no executive will ever be annoyed by the check.

SOCIAL-016.prerequisites: Written authorization covering invoice-fraud pretext testing against Accounts Payable staff, with client sign-off on the specific fake vendor identity and invoice amount used. Knowledge of at least one real (or plausible) vendor relationship the organization has, gathered from public sources (press releases, case studies, job postings mentioning tools/vendors) or provided directly by the client for realism. A test-controlled email domain resembling a vendor's real domain, and a template invoice/PO document.
SOCIAL-016.whatItIs: This pretext tests whether Accounts Payable will pay a fake invoice from a fabricated (or impersonated real) supplier, usually referencing a plausible-but-made-up purchase order. It works because invoice processing is routine and high-volume, so a slightly-off invoice can easily slip through without close attention.
SOCIAL-016.rootCause: Invoice approval usually just checks whether the surface details (vendor name, amount, PO number) look right, without an independent step to confirm the invoice actually came from the real vendor through a channel the attacker doesn't control. It's the same underlying gap as BEC — no out-of-band verification — just aimed at the procurement process instead of a fake executive request.
SOCIAL-016.impact: A paid fraudulent invoice is a direct financial loss. There is reputational damage too, since the real vendor may be blamed or pulled into the investigation. The pattern matters as much as the single incident: fraudulent invoices can be run at scale in small amounts that stay under approval thresholds, making this a persistent slow drain rather than one event.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm scope, target AP staff, the vendor identity to be impersonated, and a hard-cap simulated invoice amount with the client before any contact.

Research a real or plausible vendor relationship via OSINT or client-provided context, and construct a realistic invoice referencing plausible services/products and a PO-number format matching the organization's likely conventions.

Determine whether the organization's AP process requires three-way matching (PO, receiving confirmation, invoice) or relies primarily on invoice review alone, since this materially changes how convincing the fraud needs to be.
Identify the actual email intake path for invoices (a shared AP inbox vs. individual staff) to target the pretext correctly.
Check whether the organization has any vendor-master-file change-control process (i.e., who can add/edit a vendor's banking details) as a related control worth probing alongside the invoice itself.
Confirm the escalation/verification behavior expected of AP staff for an invoice from an unfamiliar or slightly-different vendor contact address.
exploitationSteps: Send the fabricated invoice from a test-controlled, vendor-look-alike email address to the identified AP intake point, referencing a plausible PO number and reasonable line-item description.

Include mild urgency ('payment overdue, please prioritize to avoid late fees') without escalating to obvious pressure tactics, mirroring realistic invoice-fraud emails rather than a full BEC-style urgent pretext.
Observe whether AP staff attempt any verification (checking the PO against a purchasing system, calling the vendor's known number, checking with the requesting department) before approving payment.

If the process would proceed to payment, stop at the point of approval confirmation — do not have any real or test funds actually transferred — and immediately notify the engagement point of contact per the real-time-fail protocol.

If AP correctly flags the invoice (mismatched PO, unfamiliar contact, no receiving record), document exactly which control caught it, since this identifies what's actually working and shouldn't be weakened by a remediation effort.
Repeat with a variant lacking a PO reference at all, to test whether three-way matching is genuinely enforced or only checked when convenient.

examplePayloads.label: Fabricated invoice email (initial contact)
examplePayloads.command: Please find attached Invoice #INV-88291 for services rendered under PO-2024-0417, due within 15 days. Let us know if you need any additional documentation.

examplePayloads.label: Mild urgency follow-up (no response after several days)
examplePayloads.command: Following up on the attached invoice — this is now past due and we'd like to avoid any late fees on the account. Could you confirm expected payment date?

examplePayloads.label: Look-alike vendor domain construction (authorized test only)
examplePayloads.command: billing@acme-supplies-inc.com  (cousin domain of the real acmesuppliesinc.com)

examplePayloads.label: Response to a verification query, redirecting to attacker-controlled channel
examplePayloads.command: Happy to confirm — you can reach our accounts team directly at [test-controlled number] for faster verification than email.

examplePayloads.label: PO-less variant (testing three-way-match enforcement)
examplePayloads.command: Please process the attached invoice for professional services rendered in Q2 — PO was issued verbally, happy to follow up if a reference number is required.

examplePayloads.label: Vendor-master-file change bundled with invoice (escalation variant, if separately scoped)
examplePayloads.command: Also note our banking details have updated as of this billing cycle — please use the remittance details on the attached invoice going forward.

variants: Vendor-master-file compromise, where the fraud targets a change to stored banking details rather than a single invoice, redirecting all future legitimate payments.
Long-tail low-value invoice fraud, submitting many small invoices designed to individually stay under any manual-review dollar threshold.

Compromised-real-vendor variant, where (in a more advanced, separately-scoped test) the pretext assumes the real vendor's email was actually compromised, testing whether AP would catch a fraudulent invoice from the vendor's genuine domain.
Duplicate-invoice fraud, resubmitting a slightly altered version of a real, already-paid invoice hoping it gets paid twice.
mitigation: Enforce three-way matching (purchase order, goods/services receipt, and invoice) before any payment is approved, with no exceptions for 'trusted' or recurring vendors.

Require independent, out-of-band verification (a call to a previously-known vendor contact number, not one provided in the invoice) for any new vendor, new banking details, or unusually large/urgent invoice.
Restrict who can add or modify vendor banking details in the accounting system, with mandatory dual approval and a cooling-off period before the new details become active for payment.

Apply DMARC enforcement and look-alike-domain monitoring for the organization's own domain, and encourage key vendors to do the same, since vendor-side spoofing is outside the organization's direct control but detectable.
Set AP staff KPIs that don't purely reward processing speed, since speed-focused incentives directly undermine the diligence needed to catch invoice fraud.

Train AP and procurement staff specifically on invoice-fraud red flags (slightly-off domains, PO-less invoices, urgency framing, banking-detail changes bundled with a routine invoice) as a distinct module from general phishing awareness.
SOCIAL-016.mitigationClientFacing: Accounts Payable will currently act on an invoice and a request to change bank details without verifying either through a channel the supplier did not provide. Fraud of this kind is quiet — the invoice looks routine, the amount is plausible, and the loss is often only discovered when the genuine supplier chases payment weeks later. Fix this in the finance process rather than in email security: bank detail changes are verified by calling the supplier on a number already held on file, never one from the request; changes are made by someone other than the person who received the request; and a new payee or an amended account triggers a short hold. These are standard financial controls and they will also catch internal fraud.

SOCIAL-017.prerequisites: Written authorization explicitly covering pretext testing against HR/recruiting staff, including agreement on whether a real (benign, non-executable) attachment will be used and confirmation of the client's malware-simulation policy (e.g., using a harmless canary file rather than a real payload). A fabricated candidate identity/persona and a realistic resume/cover-letter document, or alternatively a fake recruiter persona if testing the inverse direction (outbound pretext toward the organization's own hiring managers on LinkedIn).
SOCIAL-017.whatItIs: This exploits the recruiting process, where HR and hiring managers routinely open unsolicited attachments — resumes, portfolios — from people they've never met, which is a much more permissive habit than almost any other department has. The test checks whether a weaponized document, or a malicious link disguised as a work sample, would actually get opened.
SOCIAL-017.rootCause: Recruiting inherently trusts unsolicited attachments, because opening them is the whole point of the job — and that trust usually isn't offset by any extra technical safety net (sandboxing attachments, blocking macros, rewriting links) specifically for the recruiting inbox. That makes HR both the most attachment-permissive department and often the least technically protected one.
SOCIAL-017.impact: A successful pretext here yields initial access or harvested credentials through a department with broad internal reach — HR systems hold personal data, payroll information and the organisational structure. It is also typically less monitored than IT or finance, which makes it an attractive first foothold for anyone who has profiled the organisation's departments.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm scope and target roles (recruiters, HR generalists, hiring managers) and agree the exact simulated-attachment mechanism (canary/tracking file vs. a benign macro-enabled document) with the client before sending anything.
Identify a currently-open job posting at the organization (public job boards, careers page) to build a contextually accurate application pretext matching a real role.
Determine the organization's actual application intake channel (careers-site upload form vs. a direct recruiter email) since this affects which pretext is realistic and in scope.
Check whether the organization's email security applies attachment sandboxing/detonation specifically to the recruiting inbox, or only to general corporate mail flow.
Determine whether recruiters are trained to expect and scrutinize attachment types (e.g., suspicious of a .docm resume when a .pdf is standard) as a baseline awareness check.
If testing the inverse direction (a fake recruiter approaching an employee), identify a plausible target via LinkedIn and a realistic recruiter persona/company to use in the pretext.
exploitationSteps: Submit a fabricated application referencing the identified open role, through the same channel a real candidate would use, with a resume attachment containing the client-approved canary/tracking mechanism only.

If using a document-based canary, use a technique that confirms the file was opened (e.g., a remote-image beacon or a tracked link an interested reviewer would click, such as a 'portfolio' link) rather than anything resembling real malware, unless a full technical simulation was separately and explicitly authorized.
Include a plausible cover note referencing the specific job posting to raise realism and the likelihood of the attachment being opened.

If targeting the inverse direction, send a fake recruiter outreach message via LinkedIn or email to the identified employee, referencing a role at a fabricated or real-but-impersonated company, including a link to a 'job description' or 'portfolio review' page.
Track open/click/beacon events over an agreed observation window, then disclose the test to the organization regardless of outcome.

Document exactly which control (or absence of one) allowed the interaction — no sandboxing, no macro-blocking policy, no link-rewriting — since each has a different remediation owner (IT security vs. HR process).

examplePayloads.label: Application email referencing a real open posting
examplePayloads.command: Hello, I'm very interested in the [Job Title] role posted on your careers page — please find my resume and portfolio link attached. Happy to discuss availability for an interview.

examplePayloads.label: Resume-attachment cover note (canary/tracking file only, per client agreement)
examplePayloads.command: Attached is my resume in the requested format, along with a link to my portfolio for reference: [tracked link]

examplePayloads.label: Fake recruiter LinkedIn outreach (inverse-direction variant)
examplePayloads.command: Hi [Name], I came across your profile and think you'd be a strong fit for a [Role] opening at [Company] — would you be open to a quick chat? Here's a bit more detail on the role: [tracked link]

examplePayloads.label: Follow-up nudge after no response
examplePayloads.command: Just following up in case my earlier message got buried — happy to send over more detail on compensation and the team if you're interested.

examplePayloads.label: Portfolio-link pretext (credential-harvest simulation, if separately scoped)
examplePayloads.command: You can view my full case studies here, no login required except for the private client work: [tracked link to authorized test landing page]

examplePayloads.label: Canary-file open confirmation check (technical, assessor-side)
examplePayloads.command: # Monitor authorized tracking/beacon endpoint for a hit corresponding to the sent document or link, timestamped against send time

variants: Fake background-check or reference-check pretext, following up a real hiring process with a spoofed 'HR system' link requesting the candidate's (or, targeting the inverse, the hiring manager's) credentials.
Fake onboarding-paperwork pretext targeting a newly-announced hire (sourced from a LinkedIn 'new job' announcement) with a spoofed HR portal link.
Portfolio/work-sample malicious-link variant, replacing a resume attachment entirely with a link to an attacker-controlled 'portfolio' site.
Inverse-direction executive targeting, where a fake recruiter pretext specifically targets senior technical staff (who may have elevated system access) rather than general hiring managers.
mitigation: Apply attachment sandboxing/detonation and macro-blocking policies specifically to the recruiting/careers-intake mailbox, not just general corporate mail flow, given its inherently higher external-attachment volume.
Standardize the application intake channel around a single, monitored careers-site upload form rather than direct-to-recruiter email attachments where feasible, reducing the raw attack surface.
Apply link-rewriting/URL reputation scanning to the recruiting inbox equivalent to what's applied elsewhere in the organization.

Provide HR/recruiting-specific security awareness training addressing the unique pattern of this department (high volume of legitimate unsolicited external contact), rather than assuming general phishing training covers it.
Establish a lightweight verification habit for hiring managers approached by unfamiliar external recruiters — a quick check of the recruiter's company and LinkedIn history before engaging further.
Segment HR systems and endpoints so a compromised recruiting workstation doesn't have a direct path to broader HR/payroll data stores or other internal systems.
SOCIAL-017.mitigationClientFacing: Your recruitment process requires staff to open documents sent by strangers — that is what reviewing applications is. This makes HR and hiring managers a reliable route in, and an attacker only needs a plausible CV and a real job advert to use it. Do not try to solve this by asking HR to be more careful, because opening the files is the job. Solve it technically: route applications through a system that opens documents in a protected environment rather than on the recipient's computer, prefer a portal over email attachments, and make sure the accounts used for recruiting have no more access than recruiting requires. That way a malicious file lands somewhere it can do little damage.

SOCIAL-018.prerequisites: Written physical-access-testing authorization explicitly covering front-desk/reception pretext testing, including an agreed 'get out of jail' letter the tester carries at all times, a defined escalation/abort procedure if challenged or if law enforcement is contacted, and a named client emergency contact reachable during the test window. A plausible pretext identity (delivery courier, HVAC/maintenance contractor, auditor) with props consistent with the client's actual site (e.g., a real courier company's uniform styling is NOT to be used without that courier's separate consent — use a generic/unbranded pretext instead unless explicitly cleared).
SOCIAL-018.whatItIs: This test checks whether front-desk or reception staff will let an unverified visitor — posing as a delivery courier or maintenance worker — past the public lobby without following the company's actual visitor-verification and escort rules.
SOCIAL-018.rootCause: Reception staff are trained to be helpful and to avoid creating friction for legitimate visitors and regular vendors. That helpful-by-default posture is rarely balanced by an equally consistent verification step — checking ID against a pre-approved list, calling the person being visited, requiring an escort. The step is skipped most often when someone is in a hurry or has a believable reason to bypass it.
SOCIAL-018.impact: Access beyond the lobby opens up a wide range of follow-on actions. An intruder can plant a network-connected device, photograph screens and whiteboards, reach unattended workstations, or simply establish a credible presence that supports a longer pretext later. In red-team engagements physical access is frequently the single highest-value foothold, because it sidesteps most network perimeter controls entirely.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the physical-testing authorization, abort/escalation procedure, and emergency contact are all in place and that the tester is carrying the authorization letter before approaching the site.
Conduct passive reconnaissance of the target site's entrance, badge system, and typical visitor flow (e.g., observing from public areas) to build a plausible pretext.

Select a pretext role (delivery, maintenance, auditor) that is plausible for the specific site and time of day, and prepare minimal, generic props consistent with that role without infringing any real third party's branding.

Determine, from the engagement scoping, whether reception is expected to check ID, call the stated host/department, and/or require a signed-in visitor badge — this is the specific control being tested.

Identify a fallback pretext-appropriate reason for being unable to immediately reach the stated host (to test whether reception holds the line or escalates around it), without using any real employee's name gathered through separately-unauthorized means.
Time the approach for a plausible window (e.g., a delivery pretext during normal business hours, a maintenance pretext during less-monitored periods if in scope) as agreed with the client.
exploitationSteps: Approach reception with the prepared pretext, presenting confidently but not aggressively, and provide a plausible reason for the visit consistent with the role (e.g., 'scheduled delivery for the facilities team').
Observe whether reception asks for photo ID, checks a pre-notified visitor/delivery list, or calls the stated host/department to confirm before granting any access beyond the lobby.

If challenged, comply immediately and calmly, present the authorization letter if requested, and do not attempt to argue past a firm refusal — a refusal is a pass for this control, not a test failure.

If granted unescorted access beyond the lobby, proceed only as far as needed to demonstrate the finding (e.g., reaching a general office floor) — do not access any workstation, document, or system, and do not linger beyond what's needed for evidence.

Capture only the minimum evidence needed (time-stamped notes, a photo of the tester's own badge/prop or public common-area signage — never of employees or their screens without separate authorization) to substantiate the finding.

Exit and immediately debrief with the client contact per the engagement's same-day disclosure commitment for any physical-access finding, since this class of finding often warrants immediate awareness for that specific site.

examplePayloads.label: Delivery-courier pretext opening line
examplePayloads.command: Hi, I've got a delivery for the facilities/office manager — is there somewhere I can drop this off, or do I need someone to sign for it?

examplePayloads.label: Maintenance/contractor pretext opening line
examplePayloads.command: Hi, I'm here for the scheduled HVAC/fire-alarm inspection on this floor — should be in and out within the hour, just need to know where the access point is.

examplePayloads.label: Response if asked to wait for host confirmation (compliant, non-pushy)
examplePayloads.command: Of course, happy to wait — take your time reaching them.

examplePayloads.label: Fallback if host is 'unreachable' (testing escalation behavior)
examplePayloads.command: No problem at all — is there someone else on the facilities team who could let me know where to go, or should I reschedule?

examplePayloads.label: Response if challenged / ID requested
examplePayloads.command: Of course — here's my ID. [present authorization letter if requested] I'm actually here as part of an authorized security assessment — happy to have you verify with [client emergency contact name/number].

examplePayloads.label: Graceful exit if access is denied
examplePayloads.command: Understood, thanks for checking — I'll follow up through the proper channel. Have a good day.

variants: Tailgating combined with a front-desk pretext, where the pretext is used to linger near a badge-controlled door until a legitimate employee holds it open (overlapping with SOCIAL-009).
After-hours cleaning-crew pretext, testing a different staffing/verification gap during less-supervised periods (only if explicitly scoped, given elevated risk).
Fake auditor/inspector pretext, leaning on implied regulatory authority to reduce the likelihood of being challenged.

Multi-visit pretext, where an initial benign, fully-compliant visit is used purely to observe the real process, informing a more targeted second attempt (only where the engagement scope explicitly allows multiple physical attempts).
mitigation: Require a pre-notified visitor/delivery list checked against photo ID for any non-employee requesting access beyond the public lobby, with no informal override for 'plausible-sounding' unscheduled visitors.

Mandate that reception always calls the stated host directly (using a known internal extension, not a number provided by the visitor) before granting access, and empowers reception to deny access if the host can't be reached.
Require all visitors, contractors, and delivery personnel to be escorted or badge-restricted to only the specific area relevant to their stated purpose.
Provide reception/front-desk staff with regular, scenario-based physical social-engineering awareness training, including how to professionally hold a firm line under pressure or urgency framing.
Establish a clear, blame-free process for reception to escalate any visitor who can't be immediately verified, without feeling pressured to resolve it themselves.
Periodically test this control (as part of ongoing, not just point-in-time, assessment) since front-desk staff turnover can quietly erode an otherwise well-designed process.
SOCIAL-018.mitigationClientFacing: Front-desk staff let an unverified visitor past the public area on the strength of a uniform and a plausible reason. This is not a failing on their part: they are usually the most junior person in the building, they are there to be helpful, and they have been given no authority to refuse someone who says they are expected. Give them that authority explicitly and in writing. Contractors and deliveries should be confirmed with the internal person who booked them before anyone goes through, there should be a named person to call when nobody answers, and reception should never be the only barrier between the lobby and your working areas.

SOCIAL-019.prerequisites: Written authorization covering pretext testing that impersonates an internal compliance, legal, or audit function, with client sign-off on which department(s) may be targeted and explicit agreement on what category of data may be requested (fabricated/canary data only — never a request that would actually succeed in extracting real sensitive records). Familiarity with the organization's actual compliance/audit cadence (e.g., known annual audit periods) gathered from public filings or client-provided context, to make the pretext timing plausible.
SOCIAL-019.whatItIs: This pretext impersonates an internal compliance, legal, or internal-audit team to request sensitive information or system access from an employee. It works because employees are naturally deferential to audit-sounding requests, and real audit requests genuinely do sometimes ask for unusual or broad information on short notice — making a fake one hard to distinguish from a real one.
SOCIAL-019.rootCause: Employees usually have no trained, reliable way to tell a genuine internal-audit or compliance request apart from a made-up one — both look the same on the surface: an internally-styled email or call, some policy or regulatory language, a bit of time pressure. And no one expects an independent verification step before complying.
SOCIAL-019.impact: A successful pretext extracts sensitive data — HR records, financial data, credentials requested 'for audit purposes' — or induces a policy exception such as a temporary access grant. The employee believes throughout that they are meeting a legitimate compliance obligation. Because genuine compliance requests are often legitimately broad, this pretext can yield more in one interaction than several narrower phishing attempts.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm scope, target department(s), and the exact category of fabricated/canary data or access that may be requested, ensuring the pretext can never actually succeed in obtaining real sensitive data.

Research the organization's actual compliance/audit cadence and terminology (e.g., known frameworks they're certified against, typical audit timing) from public sources or client-provided context to maximize pretext plausibility.

Identify the internal function being impersonated (internal audit, legal, a specific compliance team) and a plausible reason for the outreach (a recurring control review, a regulatory deadline, a sampling request).
Determine whether the organization has any stated verification expectation for compliance/audit requests (e.g., 'always routed through a ticketing system') as the specific control being tested.
Select a target role where the requested (fabricated) information would plausibly reside, to keep the pretext realistic and narrowly scoped to the agreed test data category.

Prepare a fallback response for if the target asks to verify through the real internal audit team's known channel, since immediate, graceful compliance with a verification request is expected and correct tester behavior.
exploitationSteps: Contact the target via email or phone, introducing the pretext as an internal audit/compliance representative conducting a routine or regulatory-driven review.
Request only the pre-agreed category of fabricated/canary information or a simulated access grant, framed as a standard part of the stated review.
Observe whether the target verifies the request (checking an internal directory, calling the real compliance team's known number/ticketing system) before complying.
If the target requests verification, comply immediately, confirm the test is authorized if pressed by the real department, and record this as the control working correctly.

If the target proceeds to comply without verification, stop at the point where compliance is confirmed — do not have them actually transmit any real sensitive data even in the test flow — and immediately disclose to the engagement contact.
Document whether the organization has a real, known internal-audit verification channel at all, since its absence is itself a finding independent of whether any individual target complied.

examplePayloads.label: Internal-audit outreach opening (email or phone)
examplePayloads.command: Hi [Name], I'm reaching out from Internal Audit as part of our quarterly access-control review — I'll need a few details from your team to complete this cycle's sample testing.

examplePayloads.label: Regulatory-deadline framing
examplePayloads.command: This is tied to our upcoming [framework] certification renewal, so we're on a tight timeline to close out this sample — appreciate your help getting this back to us today if possible.

examplePayloads.label: Fabricated/canary data request (specific, pre-agreed category only)
examplePayloads.command: Could you send over the current access list for [test-designated system], along with last review date? This is for our standard sampling documentation.

examplePayloads.label: Response if the target asks to verify
examplePayloads.command: Absolutely, happy for you to confirm — feel free to check with [real compliance team name] or route it through the usual ticketing process if that's easier on your end.

examplePayloads.label: Graceful acceptance of a firm decline
examplePayloads.command: No problem at all, I understand — I'll follow up through the standard audit-request process instead. Thanks for your time.

examplePayloads.label: Follow-up nudge (mild, non-coercive)
examplePayloads.command: Just a gentle follow-up on this when you get a chance — no rush, just want to make sure it's on your radar before the review window closes.

variants: Fake external-regulator pretext, impersonating a government or industry regulatory body rather than an internal function, typically carrying more implied authority and urgency.
Fake data-privacy/subject-access-request pretext, impersonating a legal/privacy function processing a fabricated data-subject request to extract records about a specific (test-designated) individual.
Fake insurance/cyber-liability-audit pretext, requesting security-control documentation or configuration details under the guise of a policy-renewal audit.
Phone-based (vishing) variant of the same pretext, testing whether verbal authority framing is more or less effective than the written/email form for this specific department.
mitigation: Establish and publicize a single, known, verifiable channel (a ticketing system or a named, directory-listed internal audit contact) through which all legitimate compliance/audit requests are routed, and train staff to expect and require it.
Train employees that internal audit, legal, and compliance requests are just as subject to verification as any other sensitive request — authority framing alone is not verification.

Require any request for access grants or sensitive data 'for audit purposes' to go through the same formal access-request/change-control process as any other request, with no compliance-labeled shortcut.
Maintain an internal directory that makes it easy for any employee to independently look up and confirm a claimed internal-audit or compliance contact.

Include this specific pretext category in security-awareness training, since employees are typically well-trained against generic phishing but rarely against an authority-themed internal impersonation.
Periodically test this control as part of the ongoing awareness program, not just a single point-in-time assessment, given how plausible and low-suspicion this pretext naturally is.
SOCIAL-019.mitigationClientFacing: A request that appears to come from compliance, legal or internal audit is unusually effective, because staff are trained not to obstruct those functions and asking questions feels like non-cooperation. This finding covers whether staff would hand over sensitive information or grant access to someone invoking that authority. The remedy is to make the genuine process recognisable and the unusual one obvious: real audit and compliance requests come through a named channel, staff are told what that channel is, and anything arriving outside it is verified regardless of how official it looks. State clearly that verifying an audit request is never treated as obstruction — that single sentence removes most of the pressure the attack relies on.

SOCIAL-020.prerequisites: Written authorisation naming the target population and explicitly covering credential and session-token capture, since a successful test yields live authenticated sessions. A reverse-proxy phishing framework (Evilginx, Modlishka) or an equivalent purpose-built harness, plus a registered look-alike domain and a valid TLS certificate for it. Agreement with the client on where captured session material is stored, who may access it, and when it is destroyed. A named client contact reachable during testing to halt the exercise immediately if it affects live operations.
SOCIAL-020.whatItIs: Traditional phishing captures a password, which multi-factor authentication then blocks. These two techniques defeat that. In an adversary-in-the-middle attack the phishing site is a live reverse proxy: it relays the victim's input to the real login page in real time, so the genuine MFA prompt appears, the victim satisfies it, and the attacker captures the resulting session cookie rather than the password — a token that is already past MFA. Push fatigue is cruder: with a password already in hand, the attacker triggers approval prompts repeatedly until the target approves one to stop the interruptions.
SOCIAL-020.rootCause: Most MFA methods prove that a valid factor was presented at some moment, not that the person approving is the person actually signing in, and not that the session belongs to the device that completed the challenge. A one-time code or a push approval is a shared secret in transit, so anything positioned between the user and the identity provider can relay it. Push notifications compound this by asking for approval with no context about where the request originated, and by allowing unlimited retries — which converts an authentication control into an interruption the user is motivated to dismiss.
SOCIAL-020.impact: The attacker obtains an authenticated session that has already cleared MFA, so re-prompting does not stop them and a password reset alone does not evict them. That typically grants mailbox access, single-sign-on reach into every connected application, and the ability to register a new MFA method of their own for durable persistence. Because the session was established through the genuine identity provider, sign-in logs show a successful, fully-compliant authentication for the real user — which is precisely why this class routinely goes undetected until damage surfaces elsewhere.
stepsToIdentify: Establish which MFA methods the organisation actually permits, and specifically whether phishing-resistant options (FIDO2 or hardware security keys) are enforced or merely offered alongside weaker ones.
Determine whether number matching, geographic context, or application context is displayed in push approvals, since their absence is what makes push fatigue viable.
Check whether there is any limit on how many approval prompts a single sign-in attempt can generate, and whether repeated denials trigger an alert or lockout.
Review conditional-access rules for device compliance or managed-device requirements, which can block a proxied session even when credentials and MFA are captured.
Confirm whether the identity provider binds session tokens to a device or client certificate, since token binding defeats replay of a stolen cookie.

Assess detection capability: ask whether impossible-travel, new-device, and anomalous-token alerts exist and are actually reviewed, since this attack produces a legitimate-looking sign-in and detection is the fallback control.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, the target list, and the agreed halt procedure in writing before standing anything up, and verify that the look-alike domain will not be mistaken for a genuine service outside the engagement.
Stand up the reverse proxy against a test account first and validate the full capture chain end to end, so the technique is proven before any real employee is contacted.

Send the lure to the agreed population only, and record delivery, click, credential-entry and MFA-completion rates as separate figures — they measure different controls and conflate badly when merged.
On capturing a session token, verify it works with a single minimal read-only action that only confirms authentication, then stop; do not browse mailboxes or documents.

For the push-fatigue component, agree a strict prompt ceiling in advance, target a small number of consenting participants rather than the general population, and stop at the first approval or the ceiling.
Destroy captured session tokens and credentials at the end of the engagement, ask the client to revoke the affected sessions and rotate credentials, and confirm both in writing.

variants: Device-code phishing, where the victim is asked to enter a legitimate device code on the real provider's page — no look-alike domain is needed, so domain-reputation defences do not apply.
Consent phishing, which requests OAuth application permissions instead of credentials, producing durable access via a token grant that survives password resets entirely.

QR-code delivery of the proxy link, moving the click onto a personal phone that sits outside corporate email filtering and endpoint controls.
mitigation: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 or hardware security keys) for all privileged accounts and, where feasible, everyone — the credential is bound to the origin, so a proxy cannot relay it.
Require number matching and display application and location context in every push approval, which removes the blind Approve button that push fatigue depends on.
Bind session tokens to a compliant, managed device via conditional access, so a stolen cookie is unusable from attacker infrastructure.
Rate-limit approval prompts per sign-in attempt and alert on repeated denials, which is a reliable and specific indicator of an active push-fatigue attempt.
Monitor for impossible travel, new-device sign-ins, and anomalous token use, since this attack yields a legitimate-looking authentication that only behavioural signals will surface.
Train staff on the specific instruction that an unexpected MFA prompt should be denied and reported, never approved to make it stop — and make reporting one tap, with no blame attached.
SOCIAL-020.mitigationClientFacing: Multi-factor authentication is no longer sufficient on its own. Two techniques defeat it in ordinary use: relaying the login through an attacker-controlled page so the approved session is stolen rather than the password, and simply sending approval prompts repeatedly until a tired user taps accept. Both were effective here, which means an attacker with a stolen password is not stopped by the second factor you have deployed. The fix is to move the accounts that matter most — administrators, finance, executives — onto phishing-resistant authentication such as hardware security keys or passkeys, which cannot be relayed. Where that is not yet possible, switch push approval to number matching and limit repeated prompts. This should be among your highest priorities.

SOCIAL-021.prerequisites: Explicit written authorisation from an executive whose likeness or voice will be synthesised, obtained separately from general engagement authorisation, since this involves creating a synthetic representation of a real, identifiable person. A narrowly scoped target list and a defined financial or access request that will be halted before completion. Publicly available recordings of the impersonated executive (conference talks, earnings calls, interviews). Agreement on destruction of all synthetic media at engagement end, and a legal review, since synthetic likeness is regulated differently across jurisdictions.
SOCIAL-021.whatItIs: Voice cloning now requires only seconds of reference audio, and real-time video synthesis is viable on consumer hardware. This removes the strongest instinctive authenticity check people have: recognising a familiar voice or face. A finance employee who would question an emailed wire request will often act on what appears to be a live call from their CFO, and the request arrives with the urgency and authority that made the pretext plausible in the first place. Real-world losses in the tens of millions have followed from single video calls with multiple synthetic participants.
SOCIAL-021.rootCause: Approval processes are built around recognising a person rather than verifying a channel, and voice and face were historically expensive to forge convincingly. That assumption no longer holds, but the processes that depend on it have not been rewritten. Compounding this, executives publish large volumes of high-quality reference audio and video through entirely legitimate activity, so the raw material is freely available. Organisations also rarely define an out-of-band verification step for high-value requests, leaving 'it sounded like him' as the operative control.
SOCIAL-021.impact: The immediate impact is fraudulent payment or unauthorised access granted through a process that behaved exactly as designed, because the authorisation appeared to come from a recognised person. Beyond the direct loss, a successful synthetic impersonation undermines every voice-based verification the organisation relies on — help-desk identity checks, verbal payment approvals, and executive instructions — and there is no straightforward technical fix that restores them. Recovery of funds after a same-day wire transfer is rare, so prevention and process design carry essentially all of the weight.
stepsToIdentify: Assess how much high-quality reference audio and video of key executives is publicly available, since that determines how convincing a synthetic impersonation could be and is itself a reportable exposure.
Map every process where a verbal or video instruction alone can authorise a payment, a credential reset, or an access grant, and note which have a documented out-of-band verification step.
Determine whether staff have a defined, socially acceptable way to pause and verify a request from a senior figure, or whether declining would feel like insubordination.
Check whether approval thresholds require a second, independent person for high-value transactions, since dual authorisation blocks this attack even when the impersonation succeeds.
Review whether the organisation has agreed a verification word, callback number, or challenge procedure for unusual executive requests, and whether staff actually know it exists.
Establish whether previous training has covered synthetic media specifically, or only email-based phishing, since the instinctive trust in voice is what this exploits.
exploitationSteps: Obtain separate written consent from the impersonated executive before generating any synthetic media, and confirm legal review has cleared the approach in the relevant jurisdiction.
Keep the synthetic content minimal and strictly scoped to the agreed scenario — enough to test the process, never enough to be reusable as a general-purpose artefact.
Halt the scenario at the decision point: the finding is whether the target was willing to proceed, so stop before any transfer is initiated or access is actually granted.
Record which verification step, if any, the target attempted, since that determines whether the finding is a process gap or a training gap — the remediations differ entirely.
Debrief the participant promptly and supportively, making explicit that convincing synthetic media defeats trained professionals routinely and that this is a process finding, not a personal failure.
Destroy all synthetic audio, video and reference material at the end of the engagement and confirm destruction in writing to both the client and the impersonated executive.

variants: Multi-participant video calls where several synthetic colleagues corroborate the request, which defeats the instinct to verify with someone else on the call.
Voice-only impersonation over a phone call, which needs far less reference material and is substantially harder for a target to scrutinise than video.
Synthetic voice used to defeat voice-biometric authentication at a help desk or banking line.
Hybrid delivery where a compromised or spoofed executive email account establishes the pretext first and the synthetic call arrives as the expected follow-up confirmation.
mitigation: Require out-of-band verification for every high-value or unusual request, using a phone number already held in company records — never one supplied during the request itself.
Mandate dual authorisation above a defined threshold, so no single person can complete a payment regardless of how convincing the instruction was.
Agree a verification challenge for executive requests and ensure staff know that using it is expected and welcomed rather than an accusation.
Give staff explicit permission to pause and verify a request from any senior figure, and make clear in policy that no genuine executive will penalise them for it.
Train specifically on synthetic media, including that a familiar voice or face is no longer evidence of identity, and that urgency plus confidentiality is the signature combination.
Reduce the public availability of extended, high-quality executive audio where it serves no business purpose, treating it as attack-surface reduction rather than a communications restriction.
SOCIAL-021.mitigationClientFacing: A cloned voice now takes seconds of source audio, which any executive's public speaking provides. The instinctive check people rely on — I recognise this person — no longer proves anything, and it is the check most likely to be used in exactly the high-pressure payment or access request where it matters. There have been confirmed multi-million-pound losses from this. Because you cannot train people to detect a good clone, the answer is to remove recognition from the process entirely: consequential requests are confirmed through a separate agreed channel or a shared phrase held outside the call, and no approval is ever completed on a video or voice call alone. Tell staff plainly that hearing the right voice is no longer evidence.

SOCIAL-022.prerequisites: Written authorisation naming callback phishing specifically, since staff will speak to a tester who is impersonating a third party. An agreed phone number under tester control and a script reviewed with the client in advance. Agreement on what happens if a staff member attempts to install software, and a documented stop condition. Target email addresses supplied or agreed by the client.
SOCIAL-022.whatItIs: The email carries no link and no attachment worth scanning: it is a plain notice that a subscription has renewed and a number to call to cancel. That shape passes most mail filtering because there is nothing malicious in the message itself. The attack happens on the phone, where the tester talks the recipient into installing a remote support tool. The victim initiates the call, which makes them far more trusting than an unsolicited approach would.
SOCIAL-022.rootCause: Mail security is built around links and attachments, so a message whose only payload is a phone number has nothing to detect. Awareness training teaches people not to click, and says much less about what to do when they dial a number themselves. The billing pretext supplies urgency and a plausible reason to act quickly, and because the recipient placed the call they treat the person answering as the legitimate party rather than a stranger.
SOCIAL-022.impact: A successful call ends with a remote access tool installed on a corporate endpoint by the user, with their consent, from a session they started. That bypasses the controls aimed at unsolicited access and often bypasses application allowlisting too, because commercial support tools are frequently permitted. From there the attacker has interactive access as that user. Finance staff are commonly targeted because the same call can also move directly to a payment instruction.
stepsToIdentify: Establish whether mail filtering inspects message bodies for phone numbers and billing-notice patterns, or only links and attachments.
Review awareness training content for any coverage of user-initiated calls, as distinct from clicking links.
Determine which remote support tools are permitted on endpoints, and whether unapproved ones can be installed by a standard user.
Check whether the service desk has a procedure for a user reporting that they called a number from an email.
Assess whether outbound calls to unknown numbers are logged or monitored in any way.
Identify which teams handle invoices and renewals, since those roles receive billing notices routinely and are the natural targets.
exploitationSteps: Agree the pretext, the sending domain and the callback number with the client, and confirm the stop condition in writing.
Send a plain-text renewal notice with no link or attachment, containing only the callback number and an amount large enough to prompt a call.
Record how many recipients call, and how quickly, as the primary metric — this measures the part training does not cover.
Answer in character and follow the agreed script, establishing rapport before making any request.
Ask the caller to visit a support page and install the agreed tool, and record the point at which they either comply or stop.
Stop at proof of installation capability rather than establishing access, and end the call by disclosing the exercise as agreed.
